title: Ohm's Law
summary: The single most used relationship in the trade: voltage equals current times resistance. Learn all three forms, work real 120 V and 240 V problems, and see how Ohm's law explains voltage drop and lamp inrush.
objectives: Students will be able to state Ohm's law in its three forms and pick the correct form for an unknown.
Students will be able to solve for voltage, current or resistance with mixed units (mA, kΩ) by converting to base units first.
Students will be able to compute the voltage drop across a conductor of known resistance carrying a known current.
Students will be able to explain why Ohm's law gives different answers for a hot and a cold lamp filament and where the law does and does not apply.

sections.heading: What Ohm discovered

sections.name: Ohm's law

variables.meaning: voltage across the component (also written E)

sections.explanation: The three quantities must describe the same component or the same section of circuit. Rearranged: I = V ÷ R gives the current a voltage will push through a resistance; R = V ÷ I gives the resistance from measured volts and amps. Convert prefixes before you calculate: 250 mA is 0.25 A and 4.7 kΩ is 4,700 Ω.

sections.heading: Using the three forms
sections.markdown:
Pick the form that isolates the unknown:

- **Unknown current:** I = V ÷ R. "How many amps will this 20 Ω heater draw at 240 V?" (240 ÷ 20 = 12 A)
- **Unknown resistance:** R = V ÷ I. "The nameplate says 120 V, 8 A: what is the element resistance?" (120 ÷ 8 = 15 Ω)
- **Unknown voltage:** V = I × R. "What is the voltage drop across 0.2 Ω of wire carrying 15 A?" (15 × 0.2 = 3 V)

A reliable habit: **write the formula, write each value with its unit, convert to base units, then calculate.** Most wrong answers on exams come from plugging 250 mA into a formula as "250" instead of 0.25.

The three quantities must belong together. The voltage must be the voltage **across** the resistance you are using, and the current must be the current **through** it. In the series and parallel lessons you will see why this matters: a series resistor sees the full circuit current but only part of the source voltage.

sections.problem: (a) A baseboard heater element measures 24 Ω with an ohmmeter (circuit de-energized). How much current will it draw when connected to 120 V? (b) A 240 V water heater draws 20 A at full output. What is the resistance of its heating element?
solutionSteps: (a) Unknown is current, so use I = V ÷ R: I = 120 V ÷ 24 Ω = 5 A.

(a) Sanity check: a 15 A branch circuit could supply this one heater; three of them (15 A) would load a 15 A circuit to 100%, which is not allowed for a continuous load (NEC 210.20(A) limits continuous loads to 80% of the breaker rating).
(b) Unknown is resistance, so use R = V ÷ I: R = 240 V ÷ 20 A = 12 Ω.
(b) Field note: if your ohmmeter read 12 Ω on a de-energized element you would know it is intact. An open (burned-out) element reads OL or infinity; a shorted one reads near 0 Ω.

sections.problem: A 120 V circuit feeds a 15 A load through 150 ft of 12 AWG copper (300 ft of conductor out and back). The conductor resistance is about 2 Ω per 1,000 ft. How much voltage is lost in the wire, and what does the load actually receive?
solutionSteps: Conductor resistance R = 300 ft × (2 Ω ÷ 1,000 ft) = 0.6 Ω.
Voltage drop V = I × R = 15 A × 0.6 Ω = 9 V.

Percent drop = 9 ÷ 120 = 7.5%, well above the 3% that the NEC informational notes (210.19 and 215.2) recommend for a branch circuit. The fix is a larger conductor (10 AWG has about 1.2 Ω per 1,000 ft, giving 0.36 Ω, a 5.4 V or 4.5% drop; 8 AWG does better still).
sections.answer: 9 V dropped in the conductors; the load sees about 111 V (7.5% drop), so upsize the conductors.

sections.heading: Voltage drop is Ohm's law on a wire
sections.markdown:
Every conductor is a resistor. Its resistance is small, but at 15, 20 or 100 A even a fraction of an ohm drops real voltage. Ohm's law on the wire alone, **V_drop = I × R_wire**, tells you how much.

Why you care:

- Motors run hot and draw more current at reduced voltage; lighting dims; electronics misbehave.
- The NEC recommends (in informational notes to 210.19(A) and 215.2(A)) keeping branch-circuit drop to about 3% and the combined feeder plus branch circuit to about 5%. California's Building Energy Efficiency Standards (Title 24, Part 6) go further and make voltage-drop limits mandatory for many nonresidential feeders and branch circuits, so check the current edition on commercial work.
- Remember to count the conductor length **both ways** (out on the hot, back on the neutral) for single-phase circuits.

The cure for excessive drop is always lower resistance: a larger conductor, a shorter run, or a higher system voltage so the same power needs less current (the next lessons explain why).

sections.heading: Where Ohm's law bends: temperature and nonlinear loads
sections.markdown:
Ohm's law assumes resistance is constant. In the real world:

- **Incandescent filaments** start cold at perhaps one-tenth to one-fifteenth of their hot resistance. At the instant of switch-on a 100 W lamp can draw 10 A or more for a few milliseconds, then settle to 0.83 A as the filament heats. That inrush is why lamp circuits pit switch contacts over time.
- **Motors** at standstill draw locked-rotor current, often 5 to 8 times their running current, because at zero speed there is no back-EMF to oppose the supply. Ohm's law still holds at every instant, but the effective opposition changes with speed.
- **LED drivers, variable-frequency drives and chargers** are electronic loads. Their current does not scale linearly with voltage; some draw *more* current when voltage sags because they regulate their output power.
- **Semiconductors** (diodes, transistors) conduct only above a threshold voltage. Ohm's law describes the resistive parts around them, not the device itself.

For sizing conductors and overcurrent protection the NEC gives you tables that already account for these behaviors (for example motor full-load current tables in Article 430 are used instead of nameplate amps). Ohm's law is the tool for the resistive parts: heaters, conductors, lamps and troubleshooting arithmetic.

**Field tip:** before measuring a low resistance, touch your meter leads together. A reading of 0.2 to 0.5 Ω is normal lead resistance; subtract it (or use the meter's relative/zero function) when you measure elements, motor windings or conductors. A cheap lead problem looks exactly like a bad element if you skip this.

sections.text: Common mistakes: (1) forgetting to convert mA to A or kΩ to Ω before multiplying; (2) using the source voltage with a resistor that only sees part of it (series circuits); (3) measuring resistance on a live circuit or through parallel paths; (4) treating nameplate watts as if they were ohms. Write the formula with units every time until it is automatic.

Open the virtual bench exercise "Series basics" after this lesson. Change the source voltage and watch the current update; then change a resistor value. Predict the new reading with Ohm's law before you look at the solver's answer.

practice.prompt: A 24 V control transformer feeds a coil whose resistance is 8 Ω. What current flows?
A load on a 120 V circuit draws 10 A. What is its resistance?
A current of 2 A flows through a 30 Ω resistor. What voltage is across the resistor?
A 9 V battery is connected across a 4.7 kΩ resistor. Find the current in milliamps.
The voltage across a fixed resistor is doubled. The current through it:
practice.explanation: I = V ÷ R. With R fixed, current is directly proportional to voltage, so doubling V doubles I.

practice.prompt: A 240 V heating element has a resistance of 48 Ω. What current does it draw?
A current of 250 mA flows through a 480 Ω resistor. The voltage across the resistor is:
practice.explanation: Convert 250 mA to 0.25 A, then V = 0.25 A × 480 Ω = 120 V. The 120,000 V answer is what you get by forgetting the conversion.

questions.prompt: A 16 Ω load is connected to 120 V. What current flows?
A current of 0.5 A flows through a 220 Ω resistor. What is the voltage across it?
A 12 V source pushes 0.5 A through a lamp. What is the lamp's hot resistance?
What current flows through a 1 kΩ resistor connected to 5 V?
Which rearrangement of Ohm's law is correct?
questions.explanation: From V = I × R, dividing both sides by I gives R = V ÷ I.

questions.prompt: A feeder carries 20 A through conductors with a total resistance of 0.15 Ω. What is the voltage drop in the conductors?
questions.explanation: V_drop = I × R = 20 A × 0.15 Ω = 3 V.

questions.prompt: Which statement about an incandescent lamp is TRUE?
choices: Its filament resistance is highest when cold, so inrush current is small
Its filament resistance is lowest when cold, so switch-on current is much higher than running current
Its resistance never changes, so Ohm's law gives the same current at all times
It has no resistance once lit
questions.explanation: Metal filaments have a positive temperature coefficient. Cold resistance is a small fraction of hot resistance, so inrush is many times the steady current.

questions.prompt: A 480 V resistive process heater has a resistance of 40 Ω. What current does it draw?
With the source voltage held constant, the resistance of a circuit is doubled. The current:
questions.explanation: Current is inversely proportional to resistance. Twice the ohms, half the amps.
